meta.title: Dutch B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Dutch → English (see the Dutch, recall the meaning) and English → Dutch (see an English meaning, recall the Dutch). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words of Dutch for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling where the language is spoken, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences, events, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Dutch has examinations at these levels — the inburgeringsexamen, the Staatsexamen NT2 and the CNaVT — but no graded word list for them was found published, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 340 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and careers, education, the media and communication, society and politics, the environment, housing, health and wellbeing, travel and transport, money, relationships and feelings, giving an opinion and arguing a point, describing things and people, culture and free time, and the verbs of change and process — and the other 660 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Dutch, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a verb or an adjective added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword has its pronunciation beneath it in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own. The 479 nouns are printed with their article — de or het — because nothing in a Dutch noun says which it takes, and they show their plural and diminutive; the 297 verbs show their past and past participle (eten, at, gegeten), and behind the All forms fold their present and past by person, imperative and participles. Real example sentences come with 990 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 949 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
